chapter.name: PythonTap Tutorial 1: A Gain, per Sample and per Vector
chapter.header: PythonTap Tutorial 1: A Gain, per Sample and per Vector
chapter.subhead: A Python class as an audio object
chapter.body: tap.python~ runs a Python class as an audio object. The class lives in a file in the PythonTap package's python folder; the object loads it, makes attributes of its typed fields and messages of its methods, and calls its process() method on the signal. In this tutorial a gain — the smallest audio object there is — is written two ways, and then you write your own.
Open the tutorial patcher, and turn on the audio with the speaker.

The left object, [tap.python~ default], loads python/default.py and makes an object of the class default in it — the file, the class and the argument share one name. Here is the part that matters (open the file in any text editor to see the rest):

The field gain, annotated float, is an attribute of the object: the attrui above it sets it, and so would the message gain 0.5 or gain 0.5 typed into the object box. Its public methods are messages: float 0.5 calls the class's method named float, and greet max prints a line to the Max console.

process() is hinted to take a float and return one, so the object calls it once per sample. That is the simplest way to write audio code, and the call itself is cheap — but every line of Python in it runs tens of thousands of times a second.
The right object loads numpy_gain.py, the same gain written with numpy:
chapter.code: def process(self, x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: return x * self.gain
chapter.body: Hinted with numpy arrays, process() is called once per signal vector, with the whole vector, and numpy multiplies it at C speed. Switch between the two with the message boxes and watch the CPU meter: for a gain the difference is small, but for anything with real work in it the vector form is the one that keeps up.

Save a copy of default.py in the python folder as mygain.py, rename the class inside to mygain, and type tap.python~ mygain into a new object box. Then change process() to soften the peaks — return math.tanh(x * self.gain), with import math at the top — and save: the object loads the file again, keeping gain's value, and the audio carries on with the new code. A mistake prints its traceback to the Max console, and the object outputs silence until a save fixes it.

A class's typed fields are attributes, its methods messages, and its process() method runs on the signal: once per sample when hinted with floats, once per vector when hinted with numpy arrays. Saving the file reloads it in place.
